    Reference

    Last updated on 2026-11-27 | Edit this page

    Working definitions

    • Sustainability: keeping useful work and its responsibilities supportable as conditions change; this may include a planned ending.
    • Governance: rules for decisions, participation, responsibility, and disagreement.
    • Stakeholder: a person or group affected by a decision or able to affect it.
    • Resources: money, staff or volunteer time, review, documentation, skills, and institutional commitments.
    • Technology: the services and tools used to publish, receive contributions, and recover work.
    • Community Engagement: learning from affected people and making their participation possible within stated support limits.
    • Citation: information identifying and crediting a particular release.
    • Preservation: retaining the artifact and information needed to interpret it; not a promise of continued operation.
    • Operation: the ongoing work of keeping a service available and supported.

    ITAV source and adaptation

    LYRASIS, It Takes a Village: Open Source Software Sustainability, February 2018, CC BY 4.0. The upload path has a later date. Printed pages 8–10 explain facets and phases; Appendix A, printed page 41 is a four-facet sustainability assessment, not a governance-model selection procedure.

    This lesson uses that edition’s phase labels: Getting Started; Growing/Getting Established; Stable, But Not Static. Assess each facet using evidence and uncertainty. Phases can differ across facets and change over time. The later ITAV toolkit supplies further official activities and sometimes different wording. Do not silently mix editions.

    The fictional case, operational rules, comparisons, and checklist are lesson adaptations informed by ITAV. They are not validated scores or official ITAV instruments. Extension beyond heritage software is a teaching choice. Official sources checked 25 November 2026.

    Governance names after the decision rule

    Name Dimension and possible benefit Question the name does not answer
    Founder authority (sometimes BDFL) A clear final decision maker can act quickly Who can challenge a decision or cover departure?
    Consensus A defined objection-resolution process can build agreement What counts as consent and how does a deadlock end?
    Contribution-based influence (sometimes meritocratic) Responsibility can follow demonstrated work Which contributions count, and who has access to contribute?
    Foundation support An organizational home may supply continuity Which decisions belong to the foundation or project team?

    These dimensions can coexist. Voting specifies an electorate and threshold; consensus specifies treatment of objections. Either needs an explicit process, record, and fallback.

    UC OSPO academic companion

    Selected readings are pinned to playbook snapshot 5636159. They are optional, not prerequisites. Campus-process descriptions are educational guidance, not approved policy. Refer licensing questions to the local technology-transfer or legal office, funding acceptance to research administration, and preservation questions to the library or repository service. Confirm local responsibilities before committing.

    Playbook category ITAV connections Selected use
    Discoverability Technology, Community Engagement; Governance for reuse responsibilities Scholarly preservation: identify a release, distinguish storage from support
    Funding Resources and Governance Funding introduction: locate commitments and referral questions
    Community Community Engagement and Governance Community introduction and communication: choose support limits and participation routes
    Product design Technology, Community Engagement, and Resources Consider contribution and maintenance costs through this lesson’s supplied profiles

    This crosswalk is an editorial aid, not a validated one-to-one mapping. The governance and project-management pages on main were rechecked on 25 November 2026 and still contain headings only. Codebase and contribution design are also draft placeholders. Do not assign them as required procedure. Recheck draft readiness before release. Prefer a channel appropriate to users, accessibility, time zones, and capacity; do not make meetings a universal rule.

    The 2026 UC contributor survey makes time and documentation relevant local priorities. Uneven recruitment and self-reports limit generalization; the study does not identify the most effective support intervention. Protected time was not offered as a support option, so reported preferences cannot rank grants against workload allocation.

    Selected teaching evidence

    • Greg Wilson, Teaching Tech Together: practical design and feedback guidance. It does not evaluate this workshop.
    • Sinha and Kapur (2021), When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: some problem-first designs benefit learning under particular conditions. Use bounded attempts with consolidation, not unsupported discovery; direct transfer to this workshop is untested.
    • Dieterich, Rumann, and Rodemer (2025), Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: effects depend on prompts, explanations, and prior knowledge. Our repair prompt follows a sound example.
    • Agarwal, Nunes, and Blunt (2021), Retrieval Practice Consistently Benefits Student Learning: broader classroom evidence supports retrieval practice, with task and setting limits. A short adult workshop still needs its own retention and application checks.

    These annotations and the 15-source research review supplied with this revision distinguish empirical findings from design guidance. No source establishes this lesson’s effectiveness. Reference review date: 25 November 2026.
